mainTopic: Three cases of lost deposits: the money given to the mother, the orphans' ox, and the deposited hops
overview: This amud holds three cases about a שומר whose deposit was lost, and each asks who has to pay. First, a man gave deposited money to his mother, who kept it in a chest instead of burying it, and it was stolen. רבא rules that the son swears he gave it to her and she swears it was stolen from the chest, and nobody pays. Second, an אפוטרופוס bought an ox for יתומים and gave it to a cowherd, but the ox had no teeth and starved. The יתומים got their money back from the seller, so the seller is the one with a claim. Since he was a trader who did not know about the defect, he swears, and the cowherd pays him the cheap value of the meat. Third, a שומר told his brewer to use his own hops, but the brewer used the deposited hops instead. The גמרא shows that both men have a defense, and that the שומר gained nothing from the hops, because the beer turned to vinegar (רב סמא בריה דרבא) or the hops were mixed with thorns (רב אשי). The ruling on the hops case continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The שומר's defense: depositors expect the family to help guard
steps.stepSummary: The שומר defends himself by saying that anyone who deposits something already expects the שומר's wife and children to look after it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Anyone who deposits something with another person does it knowing that his wife and children will also be involved in guarding it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא is checking whether to make the שומר pay. The שומר answers that he was allowed to hand the money to his mother.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A שומר is normally not allowed to hand a deposit to someone else. This line says that family members are an exception: the owner expects them to be involved. So giving the money to his mother was not a wrongful handover.

keyTerms.meaning: The person who deposits an item with a שומר
His wife and his children (the household)

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets a basic rule: a שומר may give a deposit to members of his household without being considered negligent for handing it over.

phrases.english: Anyone who deposits, with the awareness of his wife
phrases.notes: "His" means the שומר's household, not the owner's.

phrases.english: and his children he deposits.

steps.triggerLanguage: כׇּל הַמַּפְקִיד, עַל דַּעַת אִשְׁתּוֹ וּבָנָיו הוּא מַפְקִיד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the idea, raised just before this text, of making the שומר pay.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Legal principle that permits the handover
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The שומר should pay because he handed the deposit to someone else.
steps.terutzMaskana: Handing it to family is expected by the owner, so the שומר is not negligent for that.

steps.title: Should the mother pay instead?
steps.stepSummary: רבא considers making the mother pay, since she is the one who did not guard the money properly.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let us say to his mother: Go and pay.
steps.whatsHappening: The שומר got off the hook, so רבא now tries the next person, the mother. This line sets up her answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The mother put the money in a chest instead of burying it, which is not proper guarding for money. So she looks like the one who was careless.

phrases.english: Let us say to his mother: Go and pay.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Since the שומר is excused, the liability shifts to the mother.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Can the mother be held liable for the loss?

steps.title: The mother's defense: nobody told me it wasn't his
steps.stepSummary: The mother answers that her son never told her the money belonged to someone else. If she had known, she would have buried it.
steps.simpleTranslation: She can say: He did not tell me that it was not his, so that I would bury it.
steps.whatsHappening: The mother pushes back. She says she had no reason to guard the money extra carefully, because she thought it was her son's.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Her carelessness came from missing information. She only treated it like family money, so she cannot be blamed for not guarding it like someone else's deposit.

phrases.english: She says: He did not tell me
that they are not his, so that I would bury them.
phrases.notes: Earlier on this דף the גמרא taught that money is properly guarded by burying it in the ground.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the idea that the mother must pay.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: She was never told the money belonged to others, so she had no duty to guard it at the higher level.

steps.title: Back to the שומר: why didn't you tell her?
steps.stepSummary: רבא turns back to the שומר and asks why he did not tell his mother the money belonged to someone else.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let us say to him: Why did you not tell her?
steps.whatsHappening: Since the mother's excuse is that nobody told her, the blame seems to fall back on the שומר for not telling her.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The mother's defense creates a new attack on the son. He may hand the deposit to family, but maybe he was negligent for not warning her what it was.

phrases.aramaic: נֵימָא לֵיהּ: אַמַּאי לָא אֲמַרְתְּ לַהּ?
phrases.english: Let us say to him: Why did you not tell her?

steps.triggerLanguage: נֵימָא לֵיהּ: אַמַּאי לָא אֲמַרְתְּ לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the mother's defense to attack the שומר again.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Even if he could give it to family, failing to tell her it was someone else's money caused it to be guarded poorly.

steps.title: The שומר's answer: she guards my money even better
steps.stepSummary: The שומר says that not telling her was even better, because a mother is more careful with her own son's money.
steps.simpleTranslation: He can say: All the more so! When I tell her it is mine, she is even more careful with it.
steps.whatsHappening: The שומר defends his silence. He says that hiding the truth actually made her guard it more carefully, not less.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His argument is that a mother cares more about her son's money than about a stranger's. So his silence was not negligence. If anything, it helped.

phrases.english: He says: All the more so,
for when I tell her that they are mine,
she is more careful with them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Flips the challenge: the silence was a benefit
steps.terutzMaskana: Not telling her made her more careful, so the שומר is not at fault.

steps.title: רבא's ruling: both swear and nobody pays
steps.stepSummary: רבא concludes that the שומר swears he gave the money to his mother, the mother swears she put it in the chest and it was stolen, and the שומר is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: He swears that he gave that money to his mother, and his mother swears that she put that money in the chest and it was stolen, and he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: Every attempt to make someone pay has been answered, so רבא gives the final ruling: each one swears to his or her part, and no one pays.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Neither person was negligent: the son was allowed to give it to family, and the mother didn't know it needed burying. The oaths confirm that the facts really happened this way, and then the שומר is free from paying.
steps.whatToRemember: A שומר may give a deposit to his household. If he did not tell them it belonged to someone else and it was stolen while they guarded it their normal way, each swears to what happened and nobody pays.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that liability depends on actual negligence. When each person acted reasonably based on what they knew, oaths settle the facts and nobody pays.

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
He swears that those coins
he handed them over to his mother,
and his mother swears that those coins
she placed them in the chest and they were stolen, and he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After all the defenses hold up, gives the final ruling.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The שומר swears he gave it to his mother, she swears it was put in the chest and stolen, and the שומר is exempt from paying.

steps.title: The story of the orphans' ox that died
steps.stepSummary: An אפוטרופוס bought an ox for יתומים and gave it to a cowherd. The ox had no teeth to eat with, so it died.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a guardian of orphans who bought an ox for them and handed it to the cowherd. The ox had no molars or teeth to eat with, and it died.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a new story that sets up a court case. Nothing has been asked yet; this just lays out the facts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Three people are involved: the אפוטרופוס who bought the ox, the cowherd who was watching it, and the seller, who comes up later. The ox died because of a hidden problem: it had no teeth.

keyTerms.meaning: A guardian who manages someone else's property, here for orphans
A cowherd, the one who looks after the cattle

phrases.english: There was a certain guardian of orphans
who bought an ox for the orphans
and handed it over to the cowherd.

phrases.aramaic: לָא הֲווֹ לֵיהּ כַּכֵּי וְשִׁינֵּי לְמֵיכַל, וּמִית.
phrases.english: It had no molars and teeth to eat with, and it died.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new story with the same structure as the earlier case about the money handed to the mother.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Facts of the case: an ox bought for orphans died because it had no teeth while in the cowherd's care.

steps.title: How should the judges rule?
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר חמא asks how judges should decide this case.
steps.simpleTranslation: רמי בר חמא said: How should judges rule in this case?
steps.whatsHappening: רמי בר חמא opens the discussion by asking who should pay for the dead ox. This question sets up the next steps, where each person is checked one by one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is real because no one seems clearly at fault. The next steps try each person in turn and show why each one can defend himself.

phrases.english: Rami bar Chama said:
How should judges rule in this case?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the ruling on the facts just told.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Who, if anyone, has to pay the orphans for the dead ox.

steps.title: The guardian cannot be made to pay
steps.stepSummary: We might tell the אפוטרופוס to pay, but he answers that he handed the ox to the cowherd.
steps.simpleTranslation: Should we tell the guardian, 'Go pay'? He can say: I handed it to the cowherd.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא suggests making the אפוטרופוס pay and immediately pushes it away with his defense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The אפוטרופוס did what a guardian is supposed to do: he gave the ox to a cowherd to look after. Once the ox was in the cowherd's hands, its daily care was not his job.

phrases.english: Should we say to the guardian: Go pay?
He can say: I handed it over to the cowherd.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries the first possible answer to רמי בר חמא's question.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The guardian properly passed the ox to a cowherd, so he was not negligent.

steps.title: The cowherd also defends himself
steps.stepSummary: We might tell the cowherd to pay, but he answers that he put the ox with the others, gave it food, and did not know it was not eating.
steps.simpleTranslation: Should we tell the cowherd, 'Go pay'? He can say: I put it with the other oxen and threw food in front of it. I did not know that it was not eating.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא suggests making the cowherd pay and pushes that away with his defense too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The cowherd treated this ox like every other ox and gave it food. The problem was hidden in the ox's mouth, so he says he could not have known.

phrases.english: Should we say to the cowherd: Go pay?
He can say: I placed it together with the other oxen,
I threw food in front of it,
I did not know that it was not eating.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the אפוטרופוס is cleared, the גמרא tries the next person, the cowherd.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects making the cowherd pay, for now.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The cowherd fed the ox normally and could not have known it was not eating.

steps.title: A paid watchman should have checked
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: the cowherd is a paid שומר for the יתומים, so he should have checked whether the ox was eating.
steps.simpleTranslation: But after all, the cowherd is a paid watchman for the orphans! He should have checked.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the cowherd's excuse. A paid שומר cannot just say 'I didn't know.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: A שומר שכר has a higher duty of care than an ordinary person. Throwing food in front of the ox is not enough; he should have watched whether it actually ate. That would make him liable.

keyTerms.meaning: A paid watchman, who must guard carefully
To check, to look into it

phrases.aramaic: מִכְּדֵי בַּקָּרָא שׁוֹמֵר שָׂכָר דְּיַתְמֵי הוּא!
phrases.english: After all, the cowherd is a paid watchman of the orphans!
He should have checked.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִכְּדֵי בַּקָּרָא שׁוֹמֵר שָׂכָר דְּיַתְמֵי הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the cowherd's defense from step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: The cowherd's claim that he is exempt because he did not know the ox was not eating.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A paid watchman must actively check on the animal, so not knowing is itself negligence.

steps.title: The orphans did not lose anything
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא agrees that the cowherd would pay if the יתומים had lost money. But here they lost nothing, because they found the seller and got their money back.
steps.simpleTranslation: If there were a loss to the orphans, that is true. But what case are we dealing with here? One where the orphans have no loss, because they found the ox's original owner and took their money back from him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts the challenge but explains that, in this case, the יתומים were never actually hurt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא agrees a paid שומר should have checked, so he would normally pay. But the ox was sold with a hidden defect, so the יתומים took their money back from the seller. With no loss to the יתומים, there is nothing for the cowherd to pay them.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? It introduces a narrower case

steps.whatToRemember: Nobody is cleared on principle: the paid cowherd should have checked. He only escapes paying here because the יתומים already got their money back from the seller.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the גמרא is saying the cowherd did nothing wrong. It agrees he should have checked; he is exempt only because there is no loss left to pay for.

phrases.aramaic: אִי אִיכָּא פְּסֵידָא דְיַתְמֵי. הָכִי נָמֵי,
phrases.english: If there were a loss to the orphans, that would indeed be so,
but what case are we dealing with here?
One where there is no loss to the orphans,
because they found the owner of the ox,
phrases.notes: He means the man who sold them the ox.

phrases.english: and the orphans took the money back from him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 11 by limiting the case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Agrees with the principle but narrows the case to one with no loss.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A paid cowherd who did not check is liable for the dead ox.
steps.terutzMaskana: He would be liable if the orphans had lost money, but here they got their money back from the seller, so there is nothing to pay.
steps.whyThisMatters: It sets up the next question: since the seller returned the money, what happens between the seller and the cowherd?

steps.title: Then who has a claim against the cowherd?
steps.stepSummary: Since the יתומים lost nothing, the גמרא asks who is actually suing the cowherd.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, who is making a claim?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא just said the יתומים lost nothing. Now it asks who, then, has any claim against the cowherd. This sets up the next move.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The orphans are out of the picture because they got their money back. But someone still lost out when the ox died, and the גמרא wants to find that person.

phrases.english: Rather, who is making a claim?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on the answer that the יתומים lost nothing.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which party actually has a claim against the cowherd.

steps.title: The seller of the ox is the one claiming
steps.stepSummary: The seller, who had to give back the money, claims that the cowherd should have told him the ox was not eating.
steps.simpleTranslation: The owner of the ox is the one claiming. He says: You should have told us!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the ox's original owner, the seller, is the one with the claim. He says the cowherd should have let him know the ox was not eating.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The seller returned the money and now ends up with a dead ox. His complaint is that if the cowherd had told him in time, he would not have suffered this loss.

keyTerms.meaning: The owner of the ox (here, the seller)
To inform us, to let us know

phrases.english: The owner of the ox is the one claiming.
phrases.notes: He means the man who sold the ox to the יתומים and had to give back their money.

phrases.english: He should have told us!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of who the claimant is.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The seller is the claimant, arguing the cowherd should have informed him that the ox was not eating.

steps.title: The cowherd answers that the seller already knew
steps.stepSummary: The cowherd says there was nothing to tell, because the seller knew the sale was a mistaken sale.
steps.simpleTranslation: What would we have told him? He knows well that it is a mistaken sale.
steps.whatsHappening: The cowherd pushes back on the seller's claim. He says the seller already knew the ox was defective, so telling him would have added nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ox had a defect from before the sale. The cowherd argues that the seller knew this, so he cannot complain that nobody warned him.

keyTerms.meaning: A mistaken sale, a sale that can be canceled because of a hidden defect

phrases.english: What would we have told him?
He knows well that it is a mistaken sale.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the seller's claim from step 14.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The seller's claim that he should have been informed.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The seller already knew about the defect, so informing him would add nothing.

steps.title: The seller was a trader who did not know
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the seller was a dealer who buys and resells quickly, so he really may not have known about the defect.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is about a trader who buys from here and sells to there.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the seller's claim. It explains that the seller was a trader who passes animals along quickly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The cowherd's answer assumed the seller knew the ox well. A trader who buys and resells right away may never have noticed the defect, so the seller's claim still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: A trader, a dealer who buys and resells

phrases.english: With a trader who buys from here
and sells to there,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the cowherd's argument from step 15 by redefining who the seller was.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case to a specific kind of seller
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The seller surely knew the ox was defective, so he has no claim.
steps.terutzMaskana: The seller was a trader who may truly not have known.

steps.title: The trader swears and the cowherd pays the cheap meat price
steps.stepSummary: The trader swears he did not know, and the cowherd pays him the value of the meat at a low price.
steps.simpleTranslation: Therefore, the trader swears that he did not know, and the cowherd pays the value of the meat at a cheap price.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the final ruling for the ox case. The trader takes an oath that he did not know, and then the cowherd pays.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The oath confirms the trader's claim that he did not know about the defect. The cowherd does not pay the full price of a live ox, only the value of its meat at the cheap price.

keyTerms.meaning: The value of meat at a cheap price

steps.whatToRemember: The cowherd ends up paying the seller, not the יתומים, and only the cheap value of the meat, after the seller swears he did not know about the defect.

phrases.aramaic: הִלְכָּךְ מִישְׁתְּבַע אִיהוּ דְּלָא הֲוָה יָדַע,
phrases.english: Therefore, he swears that he did not know,
phrases.notes: "He" is the trader who sold the ox.

phrases.english: and the cowherd pays the value of the meat at a cheap price.

steps.triggerLanguage: הִלְכָּךְ מִישְׁתְּבַע אִיהוּ דְּלָא הֲוָה יָדַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the practical ruling from the trader explanation.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The trader swears he did not know, and the cowherd pays him the value of the meat at a cheap price.

steps.title: The story of the deposited hops
steps.stepSummary: A man deposited hops with a שומר. The שומר told his brewer to use hops from his own pile, but the brewer used the deposited hops.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain man deposited hops with his friend. The friend also had his own pile of hops. He told his brewer: Use from this one. The brewer went and used from the other one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new story about a שומר. It lays out the facts that the next steps will discuss.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two piles of hops: the depositor's pile and the שומר's own pile. The שומר pointed to his own pile, but the brewer used the depositor's hops. The question will be who must pay for them.

phrases.aramaic: הָהוּא גַּבְרָא דְּאַפְקֵיד כְּשׁוּתָא גַּבֵּי חַבְרֵיהּ,
phrases.english: A certain man deposited hops with his friend,

phrases.aramaic: הֲוָה לֵיהּ לְדִידֵיהּ נָמֵי כַּרְיָא דִכְשׁוּתָא.
phrases.english: and he himself also had a pile of hops.
phrases.notes: "He himself" is the friend who was watching the hops.

phrases.english: He said to his brewer: Throw in from this one.
He went and threw in from the other one.
phrases.notes: "The other one" is the pile that belonged to the man who deposited it.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא גַּבְרָא דְּאַפְקֵיד כְּשׁוּתָא גַּבֵּי חַבְרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new case after the ox case is finished.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets out the facts: the brewer used the deposited hops instead of the pile the שומר pointed to.

steps.title: רב עמרם asks how judges should decide
steps.stepSummary: רב עמרם asks how judges should rule in the hops case.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב עמרם said: How should judges rule in this case?
steps.whatsHappening: רב עמרם asks how a court should decide this case. This sets up the next steps, which test each possible person who might have to pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This works just like רמי בר חמא's question in the ox case. Both people involved have a reasonable excuse, so it is not clear who should pay.

phrases.english: Rav Amram said:
How should judges rule in this case?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the ruling on the case just described.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Who, if anyone, must pay for the deposited hops.

steps.title: The שומר says he told the brewer which pile to use
steps.stepSummary: If we tell the שומר to pay, he answers that he told the brewer to use his own pile.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let us tell the שומר: Go pay. He says: I told him to use from this pile.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries making the שומר pay. It then shows his defense: he gave a clear instruction to use his own hops.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The שומר says he did nothing wrong. He pointed to his own pile, and it was the brewer who used the wrong one.

phrases.english: Let us tell him himself: Go pay,
phrases.notes: "Him himself" is the שומר who was watching the hops.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר: אֲנָא אָמְרִי לֵיהּ מֵהַאי רְמִי.
phrases.english: he says: I told him, throw in from this one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the first possible payer and shows his defense.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The idea that the שומר must pay.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The שומר gave a clear instruction to use his own pile.

steps.title: The brewer says he was never told to avoid the other pile
steps.stepSummary: If we tell the brewer to pay, he answers that he was told to use one pile, not forbidden to use the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let us tell the brewer: Go pay. He says: He did not tell me, use from this one and do not use from that one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries making the brewer pay. It then shows his defense: he was never told not to use the other pile.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The brewer says the instruction was only positive: use this pile. Nobody told him the other pile was off limits, so he does not think he did anything wrong.

phrases.english: Let us tell the brewer: Go pay,

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר: לָא אֲמַר לִי מֵהַאי רְמִי
phrases.english: he says: He did not tell me, throw in from this one
and from that one do not throw in.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Parallel to step 20, now testing the second possible payer.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The idea that the brewer must pay.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The brewer was never told not to use the other pile.

steps.title: The brewer's delay should have told the שומר what was happening
steps.stepSummary: If the brewer took longer than it takes to fetch hops from the שומר's own pile, the שומר should have understood he went to the deposited pile. By staying quiet, he showed he agreed, so he should be liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if the brewer took longer than it takes to bring hops from the near pile and still did not come back, the שומר showed he was fine with it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the idea that the שומר can escape paying. It points to a case where the שומר's own silence would make him responsible.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 20 the שומר defended himself: 'I told him to use my own pile.' The גמרא answers that if the brewer was taking extra time, the שומר should have realized he went to the deposited hops. Saying nothing means he agreed, and that makes him liable.

keyTerms.meaning: He revealed what he was thinking (by his actions)
It is fine with him, he agrees

steps.confusionAlert: Two different people appear here. The one who delays is the brewer. The one whose silence 'reveals his mind' is the שומר.

phrases.english: And if he delayed the amount of time
phrases.notes: The one delaying is the brewer. The time meant is how long it takes to bring hops from the שומר's own pile.

phrases.english: needed to bring it to him
and he did not bring it to him
he revealed his mind that it was fine with him!
phrases.notes: Now we are talking about the שומר. By staying quiet, he showed he was okay with using the other pile.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the שומר's defense from step 20 by pointing to his silent agreement.
steps.kashyaTarget: The שומר's claim that he told the brewer to use his own pile (step 20)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the brewer took longer than the near pile requires, the שומר should have realized he went to the deposited pile. His silence counts as agreeing, so he is liable.

steps.title: The brewer did not take extra time
steps.stepSummary: The case is one where the brewer came back without any extra delay, so the שומר had no hint that he used the deposited hops.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a case where he did not delay.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by narrowing the case. The brewer came back on time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without a delay, nothing signaled to the שומר that the brewer went to the other pile. So his silence does not show agreement, and his defense from step 20 still works.

keyTerms.meaning: In a case where (he did) not

phrases.english: Where he did not delay.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 22 by limiting the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The שומר should have noticed the delay, so his silence makes him liable.
steps.terutzMaskana: There was no delay, so the שומר had no reason to suspect anything, and his defense from step 20 still stands. Steps 24-26 then ask whether there is any real loss at all.

steps.title: What loss is there if the שומר's beer gained from the hops?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why there is any problem at all. The hops went into the שומר's beer, so he gained from them and could pay the owner from that gain.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the end, what loss is there? Didn't the שומר gain from it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא steps back and questions the whole problem. If the שומר profited from the hops, the owner can be paid back from that profit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 20 and 21 showed that neither the שומר nor the brewer can easily be made to pay for wrongdoing. But the hops improved the שומר's beer. Anyone who benefits from someone else's property must pay for the benefit, so the owner should not lose.

keyTerms.meaning: He benefits, he gains from it

phrases.english: Ultimately, what loss is there?
But he gains from it!
phrases.notes: He means the שומר. The owner's hops went into the שומר's beer and made it better.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from 'who is at fault' to asking whether there is any real loss at all.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב עמרם's whole question of how to rule (step 19)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The שומר benefited from the hops in his beer, so the owner can be paid from that benefit and no one loses.

steps.title: The beer turned into vinegar
steps.stepSummary: רב סמא בריה דרבא says the case is one where the beer spoiled and became vinegar, so the שומר gained nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב סמא בריה דרבא said: It is a case where the beer became vinegar.
steps.whatsHappening: רב סמא בריה דרבא answers the question of step 24. The beer went bad, so there is no gain to pay from.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Paying from benefit only works if there is a benefit. Once the beer turned to vinegar, the hops did the שומר no good. So the owner's loss is real, and the question of who pays comes back.

phrases.english: Rav Sama, son of Rava, said:
Where the beer became vinegar.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 24 by describing a case with no benefit.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The שומר gained from the hops, so the owner loses nothing.
steps.terutzMaskana: The beer turned to vinegar, so there was no gain and the owner really lost.

steps.title: The hops were mixed with thorns
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי gives a different answer. The hops were mixed with thorns, so they did not improve the beer at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: It is a case of thorns.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי offers another way to answer step 24. Here the beer is fine, but the hops themselves added nothing to it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב סמא בריה דרבא said the beer spoiled. רב אשי says even if the beer is fine, these hops gave it no benefit. Either way the שומר gained nothing, so the owner's loss is real.
steps.whatToRemember: The גמרא keeps the hops case a real problem. The שומר's silence proves nothing (no delay), and he gained nothing he could pay from (the beer turned to vinegar, or the hops were mixed with thorns).

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said: With thorns,
phrases.notes: The hops were mixed with thorns, so they added nothing to the beer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, separate answer to the question of step 24.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (אוקימתא), an alternative answer
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The hops improved the beer, so the שומר can pay from his gain.
steps.terutzMaskana: The hops were mixed with thorns and gave no benefit, so there is a real loss.
